text: When I got to Facebook, I knew I wanted to build. As someone who wasn't really technical, I wasn't going to be an engineer or a coder. I wanted to work with the engineers and the coders to build products.
speaker: Naomi Gleit
context: Lenny asks Naomi about her journey from landing at Facebook as employee #29 to becoming a product manager. Naomi explains that even though she started in a marketing role, she always knew she wanted to work on building products. She describes how she systematically worked toward her goal of becoming a PM by volunteering to help with product projects after her regular work hours, essentially doing the job before she officially got it.
text_ko: 제가 페이스북에 갔을 때, 뭔가를 만들고 싶다는 걸 알았어요. 기술적인 배경이 없는 저로서는 엔지니어나 코더가 될 수는 없었고, 엔지니어들과 코더들과 함께 제품을 만들고 싶었어요. 그래서 제품 관리(product management)가 저한테 맞는 역할이라고 생각했고, 항상 PM이 되는 게 제 꿈이었어요. 결국 PM이 된 건 운이 아니라는 걸 확신해요.
text_zh: 我到Facebook的时候，就知道自己想做产品。我本身不是技术出身，当不了工程师或者程序员。但我想跟工程师和程序员一起合作，把产品做出来。我觉得产品管理这个岗位很适合我，所以我一直的目标就是当PM(product manager)，我能做上PM不是运气好，是有规划的。
text_es: Cuando llegué a Facebook, sabía que quería construir cosas. Como no era muy técnica, no iba a ser ingeniera ni programadora. Quería trabajar con los ingenieros y programadores para desarrollar productos. Pensé que la gestión de productos era lo mío, así que mi sueño siempre fue ser PM (product manager) y no fue casualidad que terminara siendo PM.
key_sentence: I wanted to work with the engineers and the coders to build products.
original_text: When I got to Facebook, I knew I wanted to build. As someone who wasn't really technical, I wasn't going to be an engineer or a coder. I wanted to work with the engineers and the coders to build products. I thought product management was the right function for me, and so my dream was always to be a PM and it wasn't luck as to how I ended up becoming a PM.

vocabulary.definition: A product manager is a professional responsible for the strategy, roadmap, and feature definition of a product or product line. They act as a liaison between various stakeholders, including engineering, marketing, and sales teams.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, product managers play a crucial role in guiding the development process, ensuring that the final product meets market needs and aligns with business goals.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a blend of technical knowledge and business acumen, and is typically used in contexts where cross-functional collaboration is essential.

vocabulary.definition: Engineers are professionals who apply scientific and mathematical principles to design, develop, and maintain structures, systems, or products. They often specialize in fields such as software, mechanical, or electrical engineering.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, engineers are critical for building and implementing the technical aspects of products, often collaborating closely with product managers and designers.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a high level of technical expertise and problem-solving ability, and is commonly used in contexts requiring specialized knowledge.

vocabulary.definition: To build products refers to the process of creating tangible or intangible goods that fulfill a specific need or solve a problem for consumers or businesses. This encompasses all stages from ideation to development and launch.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and tech companies, building products is a core activity that involves collaboration among various teams, including engineering, design, and marketing, to ensure successful market entry.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase often conveys a sense of innovation and hands-on creation, and is typically used in contexts emphasizing development and execution.

vocabulary.definition: Technical refers to the specialized knowledge or skills related to a specific field, particularly in engineering, IT, or scientific disciplines. It often pertains to the practical application of theories and principles.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, particularly in tech, the term is used to describe tasks, roles, or discussions that require a deep understanding of technology and its applications.
vocabulary.nuance: While it generally denotes expertise, it can also imply complexity and may suggest a barrier for those without a technical background.

text: I ended up going, sort of the analogy, I went to the second floor most days after work, asked if there were any projects that I could help out with. It was very early days.
speaker: Naomi Gleit
context: Naomi continues explaining how she transitioned from marketing to product management at Facebook. She describes her strategy of volunteering for PM-related work after hours - literally going to the second floor where PMs worked and asking to help with projects. Because it was early days at Facebook with limited resources, there was always extra work available, allowing her to gain PM experience before formally applying for the role.
text_ko: 결국, 비유하자면 퇴근 후 거의 매일 2층에 올라가서 도와줄 프로젝트가 있냐고 물어보곤 했어요. 초기 단계라 할 일이 사람보다 항상 많았어요. 그래서 결국 몇몇 프로젝트를 맡아 프로그램 관리(program management)를 돕고 제품 피드백(product feedback)도 주게 됐어요. 정식으로 제품 매니저(product manager)로 지원할 때쯤에는 이미 몇 달 동안 자발적으로, 거의 비공식적으로 그 일을 해오고 있었어요.
text_zh: 我当时就是，打个比方吧，基本上每天下班后都会跑到二楼去问问有没有什么项目能帮上忙的。那时候公司刚起步，活儿总是比人多，永远忙不过来。慢慢地我就接了几个项目，帮着做项目管理，提一些产品建议什么的。等到我真正正式申请产品经理这个职位的时候，其实我已经义务干了好几个月了，虽然没有正式的头衔，但基本上就是在做这个工作。
text_es: Terminé haciendo algo así como... para que me entiendas, me iba al segundo piso casi todos los días después del trabajo, preguntando si había algún proyecto en el que pudiera echar una mano. Era muy al principio de todo. Siempre había más trabajo que gente para hacerlo. Y bueno, poco a poco fui agarrando algunos proyectos, ayudando con la gestión de programas, dando mi feedback sobre productos, y cuando por fin apliqué formalmente para ser product manager, ya llevaba varios meses haciendo el trabajo de manera voluntaria, casi informal.
key_sentence: I went to the second floor most days after work, asked if there were any projects that I could help out with.
original_text: I ended up going, sort of the analogy, I went to the second floor most days after work, asked if there were any projects that I could help out with. It was very early days. There was always more to do than people to do it. And so eventually I picked up a few projects, helping with program management, giving my product feedback, and by the time that I actually applied formally to be a product manager, I had been doing the job voluntarily, almost informally for a few months.

vocabulary.definition: To undergo a change from one state or condition to another.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'transitioned' often refers to the process of shifting roles, responsibilities, or strategies within an organization, particularly during periods of change or restructuring.
vocabulary.nuance: This term implies a smooth or planned change, and is often used in contexts where adaptation is necessary; it may not be suitable for abrupt or chaotic changes.

vocabulary.definition: Offering one's services or time freely for a cause or organization without expecting payment.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business or startup environment, volunteering can refer to employees or individuals contributing their skills to projects or initiatives, often to gain experience or support community engagement.
vocabulary.nuance: While it generally carries a positive connotation of altruism, it may imply a lack of formal recognition or compensation, which can be a point of contention in professional settings.

vocabulary.definition: Temporary endeavors undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, projects are often structured initiatives with defined objectives, timelines, and resources, crucial for achieving strategic goals and driving innovation.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply varying levels of complexity and scale, and is often used in contexts where collaboration and management are key; it may not be suitable for ongoing or routine tasks.

vocabulary.definition: A plan of action designed to achieve a long-term or overall aim.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, strategy refers to the comprehensive approach an organization takes to achieve its goals, including market positioning, resource allocation, and competitive advantage.
vocabulary.nuance: This term suggests a deliberate and well-thought-out approach, and is often used in contexts requiring foresight and planning; it may not be appropriate for ad-hoc or reactive decisions.

text: So I've always said that there is the biggest gap of anybody I know between what people think of Mark and who Mark really is.
speaker: Naomi Gleit
context: Lenny asks Naomi about Mark Zuckerberg's transformation in recent years, noting how he's become much cooler and more charismatic publicly. Naomi explains that this isn't actually a transformation - it's the real Mark that she's always known becoming more visible to the public. She attributes this to Mark becoming more comfortable and confident in public speaking and showing his authentic personality rather than being scripted and careful.
text_ko: 제가 항상 말해온 건, 제가 아는 사람들 중에서 마크에 대해 사람들이 생각하는 것과 실제 마크 사이에 가장 큰 간극이 있다는 거예요. 제가 지난 20년 동안 알던 마크가 바로 이 사람인데, 이제 세상도 제가 운 좋게 봐온 모습을 드디어 보기 시작한 것 같아요. 우리가 얘기해온 그 간극이 정말로 좁혀지기 시작하고 있어요.
text_zh: 所以我一直都说，在我认识的所有人当中，马克给大家的印象和他本人的差距是最大的。我觉得这就是我这20年来认识的那个马克，现在全世界终于能看到我有幸看到的那一面了。我们之前说的那个差距，现在真的开始缩小了。
text_es: Siempre he dicho que Mark es la persona con la mayor diferencia que conozco entre lo que la gente piensa de él y cómo es en realidad. Creo que este es el Mark que he conocido durante los últimos 20 años y el mundo por fin está empezando a ver lo que yo he tenido la suerte de ver. Esa brecha de la que hemos hablado realmente se está empezando a cerrar.
key_sentence: There's the biggest gap of anybody I know between perceptions and reality.
original_text: So I've always said that there is the biggest gap of anybody I know between what people think of Mark and who Mark really is. And so I think this is the Mark that I've known for the past 20 years and the world is finally getting to see what I've been lucky enough to see. And that gap that we've talked about is really starting to close.

vocabulary.definition: The process of significant change in form, structure, or appearance, often leading to improved performance or efficiency.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, transformation often refers to organizational change initiatives aimed at enhancing operational effectiveness, adapting to market demands, or integrating new technologies.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'transformation' implies a positive change, it can also suggest upheaval or disruption, particularly in contexts where resistance to change exists.

vocabulary.definition: Possessing a compelling charm or appeal that inspires devotion in others.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, charismatic leaders can motivate teams, attract clients, and foster a strong organizational culture through their personal influence and communication skills.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'charismatic' often has positive connotations, it can also imply superficiality if the charm does not translate into genuine leadership or results.

vocabulary.definition: The way in which something is regarded, understood, or interpreted by individuals or groups.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, perception can significantly impact brand reputation, customer loyalty, and employee engagement, as it shapes how stakeholders view the organization and its offerings.
vocabulary.nuance: Perception is subjective and can differ widely among individuals, making it crucial for businesses to actively manage and influence public perception.

vocabulary.definition: The perception of an individual or organization as viewed by the general public, often shaped by media, communication, and branding efforts.
vocabulary.businessContext: A strong public image is vital for businesses as it can enhance credibility, attract customers, and influence investor confidence, making reputation management a key strategic focus.
vocabulary.nuance: While a positive public image can lead to increased trust and loyalty, it can also be fragile and susceptible to negative events or miscommunication.

text: And the most precious person in an organization is the disagreeable giver.
speaker: Naomi Gleit
context: Naomi is explaining the composition of Mark Zuckerberg's leadership team (called 'small group') and why it works so effectively. She references Adam Grant's framework about agreeable vs. disagreeable people and givers vs. takers. She explains that the most dangerous person is an 'agreeable taker' (nice but self-interested) while the most valuable is a 'disagreeable giver' - someone who will challenge ideas and push back when necessary because they're motivated by what's best for the company.
text_ko: 조직에서 가장 소중한 사람은 'disagreeable giver'(반대하면서도 기여하는 사람)이에요. 이런 사람들은 회사에 가장 이로운 일을 하려고 진짜 동기가 강한데, 듣기 좋은 말만 하진 않아요. 때로는 반박도 하고, 필요하면 어떤 일에 대해 싸워가며 밀어붙이기도 해요.
text_zh: 组织里最宝贵的人其实是那些"不好说话的给予者"。这些人是真心想为公司好的，但他们可能不太好相处，因为他们不会只说你爱听的话。该反对的时候他们会反对，该争取的时候他们会据理力争。
text_es: Y la persona más valiosa en una organización es el que da pero incomoda. Son esas personas que realmente están motivadas a hacer lo mejor para la empresa, pero pueden ser un poco incómodas en el sentido de que tal vez no te digan lo que quieres escuchar. Pueden cuestionar las cosas, pueden pelear por sus ideas.
key_sentence: And the most precious person in an organization is the disagreeable giver.
original_text: And the most precious person in an organization is the disagreeable giver. Those are the people who are really motivated to do what's best for the company, but they can be a little bit disagreeable in the sense that they may not say what you want to hear. They may push back on things, they may fight for things.

vocabulary.definition: Unpleasant or offensive in nature; likely to cause discomfort or dissatisfaction.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, a disagreeable person may challenge the status quo or provide critical feedback, which can be essential for growth and improvement.
vocabulary.nuance: While often viewed negatively, being disagreeable can also imply a commitment to honesty and constructive criticism, making it valuable in certain contexts.

vocabulary.definition: A person who provides something, often selflessly or generously, to others.
vocabulary.businessContext: In organizational contexts, a giver is someone who contributes resources, knowledge, or support to colleagues or the company, fostering a culture of collaboration.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'giver' often carries a positive connotation, suggesting altruism, but can also imply a lack of self-advocacy if overused.

vocabulary.definition: The act or process of combining various elements to form a whole; can also refer to the arrangement of parts in a particular structure.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, composition can refer to the structure of a team, product, or strategy, emphasizing how different components work together to achieve objectives.
vocabulary.nuance: While often used in creative contexts, composition can also apply to organizational structures and processes, highlighting the importance of synergy among elements.

vocabulary.definition: A basic structure underlying a system, concept, or text, providing support and guidance for development or analysis.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, frameworks are essential for guiding project development, decision-making processes, and strategic planning, ensuring consistency and alignment with goals.
vocabulary.nuance: Frameworks can be formal or informal and are often tailored to specific needs; they provide a foundation while allowing flexibility in execution.

text: What we found was the churn in resurrection lines were actually much larger than the new user line, which implied to us that retention and driving those two lines was actually our biggest lever to drive net growth.
speaker: Naomi Gleit
context: Naomi is explaining Facebook's legendary growth team approach and how they discovered the importance of retention. She describes their 'growth accounting' framework which tracked daily net growth as new users minus users who went stale plus users who 'resurrected' (returned after 30 days of inactivity). This analysis revealed that user retention was a much bigger factor in growth than acquisition, leading to their focus on engagement metrics like the famous '7 friends in 10 days' activation goal.
text_ko: 우리가 발견한 건 부활 라인(resurrection lines)의 이탈률(churn)이 신규 유저 라인(new user line)보다 훨씬 컸다는 거예요. 그래서 리텐션(retention)과 이 두 라인을 끌어올리는 것이 순성장(net growth)을 만드는 가장 큰 레버(lever)라는 결론을 내렸어요.
text_zh: 我们发现复活用户线(resurrection lines)的流失其实比新用户线大得多，这说明用户留存和推动这两条线的增长，才是我们实现净增长最重要的抓手。
text_es: Lo que descubrimos fue que la rotación en las líneas de resurrección era en realidad mucho mayor que en la línea de usuarios nuevos, lo cual nos indicó que la retención y el impulso de esas dos líneas era realmente nuestra palanca más importante para generar crecimiento neto.
key_sentence: Churn in resurrection lines is our biggest lever to drive net growth.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to keep customers or employees engaged and satisfied over time, preventing them from leaving.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, retention is crucial for maintaining a stable revenue stream, as acquiring new customers is often more costly than retaining existing ones.
vocabulary.nuance: While retention generally has a positive connotation, it can imply a need for improvement in customer satisfaction or engagement strategies when rates are low.

vocabulary.definition: To use something to maximum advantage or to exert influence over a situation or resource.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, companies often leverage their assets, relationships, or data to enhance performance or gain competitive advantages.
vocabulary.nuance: Leverage can imply a strategic use of resources, but it may also suggest a reliance on external factors that could be risky if not managed properly.

vocabulary.definition: The overall increase in a company's value or customer base after accounting for losses, such as customer churn or attrition.
vocabulary.businessContext: Net growth is a key performance indicator for businesses, reflecting their ability to expand while managing losses effectively.
vocabulary.nuance: Net growth emphasizes the importance of not just acquiring new customers but also retaining existing ones, highlighting a balanced approach to growth.

vocabulary.definition: Suggested or understood without being directly stated; inferred from context or circumstances.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business communication, implied meanings can influence decision-making and strategy, as stakeholders often read between the lines of reports and presentations.
vocabulary.nuance: Implied can carry a sense of subtlety, suggesting that the information is important but not overtly acknowledged, which may require careful interpretation.

text: One of my Naomi-isms is really understand, identify, and execute. That framework came from 2009 where the growth team at the time, it was fledgling and it just started, was focused on only instrumenting data.
speaker: Naomi Gleit
context: Naomi is sharing one of her key frameworks for product development. She explains that in 2009, Facebook's growth team realized they lacked the data needed to make informed decisions about growth levers. So they stopped all other work to focus exclusively on 'instrumenting data' - adding tracking and measurement to every step of user flows like registration and onboarding. This 'understand, identify, execute' approach became fundamental: first understand through data, then identify the biggest opportunities, then execute solutions.
text_ko: 제가 자주 하는 나오미식 표현 중 하나는 "정확히 이해하고, 파악하고, 실행하는 거예요." 그 프레임워크(framework)는 2009년에 나온 거예요. 당시 성장팀(growth team)은 막 시작한 초창기 팀이라 데이터 계측(data instrumentation)에만 집중하고 있었어요.
text_zh: 我有个口头禅叫"真正理解、识别、然后执行"。这个思路是2009年形成的，当时增长团队(growth team)刚起步，还很不成熟，只知道埋头收集数据。
text_es: Una de mis "naomismos" es realmente entender, identificar y ejecutar. Ese marco de trabajo surgió en 2009 cuando el equipo de growth (crecimiento) en ese momento, que apenas estaba empezando y era muy incipiente, se enfocaba únicamente en instrumentar datos.
key_sentence: The growth team was fledgling and focused on instrumenting data.

vocabulary.definition: To carry out or put into effect a plan, order, or course of action.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, executing often refers to the implementation of strategies, projects, or tasks to achieve specific objectives.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'execute' implies a sense of action and completion, it can also carry a connotation of urgency or precision in execution.

vocabulary.definition: A structured approach or system that provides a foundation for understanding or organizing complex concepts or processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a framework is often used to guide decision-making, project management, or strategic planning, providing a clear structure for analysis and action.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'framework' suggests a level of flexibility within a defined structure, allowing for adaptation while maintaining core principles.

vocabulary.definition: The process of equipping a system or application with tools and metrics to monitor and analyze its performance.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech startups, instrumenting is crucial for data-driven decision-making, as it allows teams to gather insights on user behavior and system efficiency.
vocabulary.nuance: Instrumenting implies a proactive approach to data collection and analysis, often associated with continuous improvement and optimization.

vocabulary.definition: Choices made based on relevant data, analysis, and understanding of the situation or context.
vocabulary.businessContext: Informed decisions are essential in business, as they rely on empirical evidence and insights to minimize risks and maximize outcomes.
vocabulary.nuance: The phrase suggests a thorough consideration of available information, contrasting with decisions made impulsively or without adequate knowledge.

text: I really believe in frameworks for things that helps drive extreme clarity. I work on a lot of different projects.
speaker: Naomi Gleit
context: This is the opening quote where Naomi introduces her philosophy about the importance of frameworks and what she calls 'extreme clarity.' She's explaining a common problem in complex organizations where different people give different answers about the same project, which creates confusion and inefficiency. This leads into her concept of 'canonical everything' - having one definitive source of truth for every project.
text_ko: 저는 사안을 아주 분명하게 해 주는 프레임워크(framework)를 정말 믿어요. 저는 다양한 프로젝트를 많이 진행해요. 새 프로젝트를 본격적으로 시작할 때(ramping up)면 항상 "이 프로젝트에 대해 제가 알아야 할 걸 어디서 배우지?"라고 생각해요. 다섯 명에게 물어보면 다섯 가지 다른 답을 듣게 되는데, 그건 용납할 수 없어요.
text_zh: 我特别相信用框架来做事，这样能让思路特别清晰。我手头项目很多，经常要启动新项目的时候，我就想"我得去哪儿了解这个项目需要掌握的东西？"结果问五个人，得到五个不同的答案。这绝对不行。
text_es: De verdad creo mucho en tener marcos de trabajo para las cosas que te ayuden a lograr una claridad total. Trabajo en un montón de proyectos diferentes. Muchas veces cuando estoy arrancando un proyecto nuevo, me pregunto: "¿Dónde puedo aprender lo que necesito saber sobre este proyecto?" Le pregunto a cinco personas diferentes y recibo cinco respuestas distintas. Eso es inaceptable.
key_sentence: I really believe in frameworks for things that helps drive extreme clarity.
original_text: I really believe in frameworks for things that helps drive extreme clarity. I work on a lot of different projects. A lot of times I'm ramping up a new project, I'm like, 'Where can I learn what I need to learn about this project?' I ask five different people, get five different answers. That is unacceptable.

vocabulary.definition: Frameworks are structured approaches or systems that provide a foundation for developing or organizing ideas, processes, or projects.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, frameworks are often used to streamline project management, enhance collaboration, and ensure consistency across various initiatives.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'frameworks' imply a level of structure and guidance, they can also suggest rigidity; it's important to choose frameworks that allow for flexibility when necessary.

vocabulary.definition: To drive means to propel or motivate action towards achieving a specific goal or outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, 'drive' often refers to the ability to inspire teams to work towards objectives, enhance productivity, or push initiatives forward.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can connote a sense of urgency and determination; however, it should be used carefully to avoid implying aggression or coercion.

vocabulary.definition: Clarity refers to the quality of being clear and easy to understand, free from ambiguity or confusion.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, clarity is crucial for effective communication, decision-making, and ensuring that all stakeholders are aligned on goals and expectations.
vocabulary.nuance: While clarity is generally positive, it is important to balance it with depth and nuance, as oversimplification can lead to misinterpretation.

vocabulary.definition: Complex describes something that consists of many interconnected parts, making it intricate and often difficult to understand.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, complexity can arise in processes, systems, or projects, requiring careful management and strategic thinking to navigate effectively.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'complex' can suggest sophistication and depth, it may also imply challenges or obstacles that need to be addressed, so it should be used judiciously.
